title: India Hosts BRICS Summit This Week With Trade, AI and Payment Systems on the Agenda
excerpt: The 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13 will test whether the expanded 11-member bloc can turn shared interests into concrete economic cooperation.
body:
• India hosts the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12-13, its fourth time chairing the bloc, which now includes 11 member nations.
  • The agenda focuses on trade, supply chain resilience, AI, digital public infrastructure, energy security and healthcare — with proposed mechanisms including a BRICS invoice discounting platform and startup innovation fund.
  • BRICS nations are discussing linking fast payment systems and central bank digital currencies, with RBI Governor Malhotra calling cross-border payments an area of shared interest.
  • China's President Xi Jinping's attendance remains unconfirmed; if he attends, it would be his first visit to India since 2019.

India will host the 18th BRICS Summit at Bharat Mandapam in New Delhi on September 12-13, bringing together leaders of what has become an 11-nation bloc representing a significant share of the world's population and economic output. The summit arrives at a moment when the expanded grouping is testing whether broader membership can translate into concrete cooperation.

India assumed the BRICS chairmanship on January 1, 2026, succeeding Brazil. It is the country's fourth time leading the grouping, following stints in 2012, 2016 and 2021. Prime Minister Narendra Modi will chair the summit under the theme "Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability."

An Expanded but Divided Bloc

What began as BRIC — Brazil, Russia, India and China — has evolved considerably. South Africa joined in 2011, followed by Egypt, Ethiopia, Iran, Saudi Arabia and the UAE in 2024. Indonesia became the 11th member in 2025. Partner countries now include Belarus, Bolivia, Cuba, Kazakhstan, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Turkey, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.

The expansion has increased BRICS' international profile but complicated its ability to speak with one voice. The bloc now includes countries with sharply different foreign policy positions — Iran and the UAE, for instance, have been on opposite sides of the West Asia conflict.

"BRICS is a platform for dialogue and cooperation, and practical responses. India seeks to address shared challenges in a balanced and inclusive manner."

— S. Jaishankar, India's External Affairs Minister

India's Four-Part Agenda

New Delhi has structured its chairmanship around four pillars. Resilience addresses supply chain disruptions, climate events and health emergencies. Innovation covers artificial intelligence, fintech and digital public infrastructure. Cooperation focuses on trade, development finance and institutional coordination. Sustainability encompasses climate action, green financing and energy transition.

On trade, India is pushing work on the BRICS Economic Partnership 2030, a proposed invoice discounting mechanism for smaller exporters and the BRICS Global Value Chains Action Plan 2026-2030 aimed at diversifying supply chains and improving market access among members.

For entrepreneurs, the proposed BRICS MSME Cooperation Portal would connect businesses with financial institutions and technology centres across member countries, while a BRICS Startup Innovation Fund could provide financing to early-stage companies.

Payments and Digital Infrastructure

Cross-border payments are emerging as one of the summit's most substantive tracks. Reserve Bank of India Governor Sanjay Malhotra said in August that BRICS nations are discussing potential linkages between their respective fast payment systems and central bank digital currencies.

"Various options are on the table, but it is still at discussion stage, including CBDCs and linkages of fast payment systems," Malhotra said at an event in Mumbai.

India's UPI system is already linked with Singapore, the UAE, France, Sri Lanka and Mauritius, among others. China's Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) had roughly 1,500 participating institutions by end-2025, with daily volumes crossing $80 billion. Russia's SPFS, designed as a SWIFT alternative, serves about 600 institutions. None individually replaces SWIFT, but together they provide redundancy that is reshaping the global payments landscape.

The Xi Jinping Question

All eyes will be on whether Chinese President Xi Jinping attends in person. If he does, it would mark his first visit to India since 2019, a symbolically charged moment given the ongoing tensions along the Line of Actual Control. China is scheduled to host next year's summit, and analysts note that Beijing's interest in maintaining BRICS momentum makes attendance likely.

India's year-long chairmanship has already involved more than 350 meetings and high-level interactions across over 25 cities, according to the Ministry of External Affairs. The summit will give leaders an opportunity to assess those initiatives and chart direction for a grouping that, as a Franklin Templeton analysis put it, sits "between Global South platform and irrelevance."

What It Means for the Diaspora

For India's global diaspora, the BRICS summit carries practical implications. Expanded payment linkages could reduce remittance costs. Trade facilitation measures could benefit Indian-owned businesses operating across BRICS markets. And India's push to export its digital public infrastructure model — from UPI to Aadhaar-style identity systems — could shape the digital environment in countries where millions of NRIs live and work.

Intra-BRICS merchandise trade reached $1.17 trillion in 2024, having expanded more than 13-fold since 2003. But that still accounts for only about 5% of world trade — suggesting significant untapped potential that the Delhi summit aims to unlock.
